data-turbolinks="false"><div class="markdown-body safe-html-box__Uwc6Al"><p dir="auto"><strong>I'm also not a lawyer (there seems to be a lot of not-lawyers) here</strong>. Also I'm EU resident.</p>
<p dir="auto">IP is considered PII, it seems, however Article 6 par 1, states:</p>
<blockquote>
<p dir="auto">(d) processing is necessary in order to protect the vital interests of the data subject or of another natural person;<br>
(f) processing is necessary for the purposes of the legitimate interests pursued by the controller or by a third party, except where such interests are overridden by the interests or fundamental rights and freedoms of the data subject which require protection of personal data, in particular where the data subject is a child.</p>
</blockquote>
<p dir="auto">And I guess if IP's are used for fraud detection and or multiple login attempts blocking it falls into these categories, <em>if</em> logs are stored for a <em>reasonable</em> amount of time (and IPs don't get to other systems). Using IP's for de-anonymisation and creating shadow profiles would be illegal though. (Still bear in mind it is not-a-lawyer).</p>
<p dir="auto">Reading <em>data portability</em> section it seems that Mastodon has had it built in from the start (purpose of this article seems to be to allow futute federation and/or moving data from and to other services). Only problem I see is that no login logs (with IP's) are in this export data.</p>
<p dir="auto">If you want to consult a lawyer, I think that asking for funds to do this from members of mastodon.technology would get a good response. I see a lot of EU folks there!</p></div></div><div role="toolbar" aria-label="Reactions" class="d-flex gap-1 flex-wrap"></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></li><li class="markdown-body" data-turbolinks="false"><div class="markdown-body safe-html-box__Uwc6Al"><p dir="auto">So, it does appear non-organizations (Natural persons) who run instances are exempted:</p>
<blockquote>
<p dir="auto">by a natural person as part of a “purely personal or household<br>
activity”. This covers correspondence and the holding of<br>
address books – but it also now covers social networking and<br>
online activities undertaken for social and domestic purposes.<br>
It represents a possible widening of the exemption from the<br>
principles set out in Bodil Lindqvist (C-101/01), before the<br>
advent of social media. In this case, the CJEU noted that<br>
sharing data with the Internet at large “so that those data are<br>
made accessible to an indefinite number of people” could not<br>
fall within this exemption, which it stated should be limited<br>
to activities “carried out in the course of the private or family<br>
life of individuals”. Note also that the GDPR will remain<br>
applicable to controllers and processors who “provide the<br>
means for processing” which falls within this exemption.</p>

dir="auto">Curious to see what outcome this will have. Having been halfway through GDPR by now too, I think the most important thing should be trying not to fall into a category of organization structure that has to comply. Otherwise it could get difficult as, no matter which features the software itself might (not) have, bottom line seems that most of GDPR actually is about how the organization operating the software works. You don't per se need software that is able to support a "right to be forgotten" it'll just makes things easier. Manually deleting things would be perfect too. But if, in example,  running a mastodon instance on some shared infrastructure,  you would also have to figure out if any of your hosting providers systems or team members could have access to relevant data and make sure they comply with GDPR too - provider HTPP proxy / loadbalancer in front of your infrastructure that is able to 'identify'' actual users?</p>
<p dir="auto">Best outcome here possibly would be a basic set of rules and guidelines for instance admins on how to behave.</p></div></div><div role="toolbar" aria-label="Reactions" class="d-flex dir="auto"><strong>IANAL.</strong></p>
<p dir="auto">Quoting someone from a discussion on Mastodon:</p>
<blockquote>
<p dir="auto">Who is the designated data controller for federated information?<br>
It must be each individual instance, but the user did not agree to any data sharing with each instance.</p>
</blockquote>
<p dir="auto">Mastodon is a federated network by design and by signing up to an instance that is connected to other instances by design, you <em>must</em> agree to your data being sent to an <em>indefnite</em> number of other instances as an effect of the functioning of the federated system. This is simply how things work. If the user is not okay with that, they may join a service that is not connected to other nodes by design and therefore has a centralized entity for controlling data, such as an "offline" Mastodon instance whose responsibilities are traceable to a single organization, or a centralized service, such as Facebook.</p>
<p dir="auto">As for the risk of unsolicited data-sharing, for any Mastodon instance, either that Mastodon instance is disconnected from the network to avoid sharing data, which defies Mastodon's whole purpose, or the designated data controller of that instance is going to be burdened with sharing information with an indefinite amount of other instances and therefore an indefinite amount of other people - and that seems like something punishable by GDPR.</p>
<p dir="auto">To anyone more skilled in law than me - is the above statement a real risk? This law does not seem to take federated networks into account. It implies that there exists a centralized data controller for a decentralized network, which is an impossibility.</p></div></div><div role="toolbar" aria-label="Reactions" class="d-flex gap-1 <p dir="auto">Maybe it would be best if it was specific about what PII was transferred in that way: user name, toots, follows, what else?, but not, e.g., IP address, password, sign in/out times, … I assume.</p>
</blockquote>
<p dir="auto">New privacy policy in master reflects this.</p>
<blockquote>
<p dir="auto">“Mastodon is a federated network by design and by signing up to an instance that is connected to other instances by design, you must agree to your data being sent to an indefnite number of other instances as an effect of the functioning of the federated system.”</p>
</blockquote>
<p dir="auto">It's not quite indefinite. For follower-only and direct messages, only the recipients will receive them, and therefore making sure they're deleted is straightforward. Public posts that can be accessed and cached from anywhere, not so much, <strong>but</strong>: Public blog posts cannot be PII. The software itself isn't the problem, but the hosting.</p>
<p dir="auto">Due to the nature of this being a federated service, it is likely that all mastodon nodes will be considered both controllers and processors according to the GDPR, and as a result will require specific phrasing that constitutes a data processing agreement.</p>
<p dir="auto">I am not a lawyer but one did very much upset me about this recently. This is a massive kick in the face for Facebook, but unfortunately the kicks don't stop there. Fortunately, this is a proportionality-based regulation so unless egregious abuse occurs, it seems unlikely we will receive a Facebook-grade punishment.</p>
<p dir="auto">A fairly useful site for GDPR stuffs I've been reading has been this: <a href="https://www.netskope.com/blog/gdpr-data-processing-agreements/" class="IssueCommentBody__DGWd7U"><div data-testid="markdown-body" data-team-hovercards-enabled="true" class="markdown-body" data-turbolinks="false"><div class="markdown-body safe-html-box__Uwc6Al"><p dir="auto">The idea that federated mastodon posts constitute Personal Data is absolutely ridiculous and doesn't hold up to the facts. While it's important to be talking about these concepts this conversation seems to have devolved into straight-up FUD.</p>
<blockquote>
<p dir="auto">The GDPR applies to data from which a living individual<br>
is identified or identifiable (by anyone), whether directly or<br>
indirectly. The Directive’s test of ‘all means reasonably likely<br>
to be used’ to identify is retained.</p>
<p dir="auto">The GDPR’s recitals highlight that certain categories of online<br>
data may be personal – online identifiers, device identifiers,<br>
cookie IDs and IP addresses are referenced. In October<br>
2016 the CJEU provided long awaited clarity on the status of<br>
dynamic IP addresses in the case of Patrick Breyer v Germany<br>
(C-582/14), holding that an IP address is personal data when<br>
held by an ISP, but does not constitute personal data if held by<br>
a party that does not have the “means likely reasonably to be<br>
used to identify the individual”.</p>
</blockquote>
<p dir="auto">You HAVE to be able to draw a full link from "a mastodon post" to "a specific natural person" for it to count as <strong>identifiable</strong> data. That's the key word here. Mastodon users do not count as natural people, I would have to create a chain of data back to a real-world identity before it becomes personal information. While some people do post their full names on mastodon or take other actions to render themselves identifiable, this is a rare case and can be handled by instance admins on a case-by-case basis, not something that needs an automated process.</p>
<p dir="auto">Now, again, IANAL, and if there's information contrary to this from a <strong>reliable</strong> source (the eugpdr.org FAQ is very informal and was taken out of context) i'd love to hear about it. But until I hear otherwise, talking about federated owners being liable for content <strong>sent</strong> to them by remote users is just fearmongering, plain and simple.</p></div></div><div <blockquote>
<p dir="auto">To be clear, I'm not looking for legal advice per se. I'm raising the question "is Mastodon GDPR compliant?"</p>
</blockquote>
<p dir="auto">Does make any sense. The question is "Is the service provider compliant?". So that question is down to every instance. And as you already figured out, it looks like instances run by individuals are not concerned. <p dir="auto">1/ right to be forgotten:<br>
HTTP DELETE on <a href="http://host/@user/" rel="nofollow">http://host/@user/</a></p>
<p dir="auto">2/ archive data<br>
HTTP GET on <a href="http://host/@user/archive/" rel="nofollow">http://host/@user/archive/</a><br>
(eventually use header for specifying formats)</p>
<p dir="auto">My question is not mastodon specific but I see this project as a very good candidate for experimenting, and showcase a pattern that other projects could replicate.</p>
<p dir="auto">Regards</p>

data-turbolinks="false"><div class="markdown-body safe-html-box__Uwc6Al"><p dir="auto">I have a few thoughts here, but IANAL.</p>
<p dir="auto">One thing that we could do is give users a settings page which lists all instances that your instance is federated with, and give a way to "opt-out" of having any of those instances be able to read your information, likewise, when we federate, we should be federating:</p>
<ul dir="auto">
<li>instance URL</li>
<li>instance contact</li>
<li>instance ToS/Privacy Policy</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Such that in the list of federated instances, users can clearly find and read the information about who and how the federated instances use their information.</p>
<p dir="auto">As for access of PII, I think through the admin panel we should hide the IP Addresses and Emails, and then only reveal them based on active selection, perhaps with the entry of the account password, and upon revealing that information, add an event to the audit log: "Moderator A viewed User B's email address at Date"</p>
<p dir="auto">Furthermore, at the database level, we should use symmetric encryption to prevent users' emails from being read by SQL queries. I'm not sure if there's anything that we can do to prevent reading the emails via Rails Console (perhaps an accessor that generates the audit log event?)</p>
<p dir="auto">Likewise, we should log audit events for searches of users by email and IP address.</p></div></div><div role="toolbar" aria-label="Reactions" class="d-flex gap-1 data-turbolinks="false"><div class="markdown-body safe-html-box__Uwc6Al"><p dir="auto">I'm a bit late to this thread, but I'd like to point out that it's a bit far-fetched to say individuals running Mastodon instances are in the clear because GDPR doesn't apply to them. It's true that there is an exemption for "[data processed] by a natural person in the course of a purely personal or household activity", but what the language is trying to cover is something like keeping a personal address book. There's some further clarification in <a href="https://gdpr-info.eu/recitals/no-18/" rel="nofollow">Recital 18</a>:</p>
<blockquote>
<p dir="auto">This Regulation does not apply to the processing of personal data by a natural person in the course of a purely personal or household activity and thus with no connection to a professional or commercial activity. Personal or household activities could include correspondence and the holding of addresses, or social networking and online activity undertaken within the context of such activities. However, this Regulation applies to controllers or processors which provide the means for processing personal data for such personal or household activities.</p>
</blockquote>
<p dir="auto">There's also some <a href="http://curia.europa.eu/juris/document/document.jsf?text=&docid=48382&pageIndex=0&doclang=en&mode=lst&dir=&occ=first&part=1&cid=322419" rel="nofollow">case law</a> from the European Court of Justice where they looked at a similar section in the Data Protection Directive (which is kind of a predecessor of the GDPR):</p>
<blockquote>
<p dir="auto">As regards the exception provided for in the second indent of Article 3(2) of Directive 95/46 [the one with "purely personal or household activity"], the 12th recital in the preamble to that directive, which concerns that exception, cites, as examples of the processing of data carried out by a natural person in the exercise of activities which are exclusively personal or domestic, correspondence and the holding of records of addresses.</p>
</blockquote>
<blockquote>
<p dir="auto">That exception must therefore be interpreted as relating only to activities which are carried out in the course of private or family life of individuals, which is clearly not the case with the processing of personal data consisting in publication on the internet so that those data are made accessible to an indefinite number of people.</p>
</blockquote>
<p dir="auto">On the bright side, <a href="https://gdpr-info.eu/recitals/no-148/" rel="nofollow">Recital 148</a> should somewhat limit the fines for individuals, stating:</p>
<blockquote>
<p dir="auto">In a case of a minor infringement or if the fine likely to be imposed would constitute a disproportionate burden to a natural person, a reprimand may be issued instead of a fine.</p>
</blockquote>
<p dir="auto">(IANAL etc. etc.)</p></div></div><div role="toolbar" aria-label="Reactions" class="d-flex gap-1 flex-wrap"></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></li><li
